report:
**Conclusion: The answer is actually yes—olive leaf extract may help reduce high blood pressure, though evidence quality is limited.**

A 2025 systematic review and meta-analysis found that olive leaf extract (1,000 mg/day) may reduce systolic blood pressure by −11.45 mmHg and diastolic blood pressure by −4.65 mmHg in pre-hypertensive and hypertensive individuals. However, the authors noted limitations including variable trial quality and exclusion of non-English studies, calling for more comprehensive clinical trials to confirm efficacy and safety (https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/ptr.8509; https://www.nutraingredients.com/Article/2025/05/15/olive-leaf-extract-may-support-healthy-blood-pressure/).

Supporting this, a 2025 multicenter randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of 621 participants assessed olive leaf extract's effects on blood pressure control in patients treated for hypertension (https://journals.lww.com/jhypertension/abstract/2025/11000/efficacy_of_olive_leaf_extracts_in_controlling.17.aspx). Earlier research also reported cardioprotective properties of olive leaf extract, including blood pressure reduction, antiarrhythmic effects, and preserved coronary blood flow (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5780626/).

The proposed mechanism involves oleuropein, a key phenolic compound in olive leaves, which may lower blood pressure by reducing oxidative stress and enhancing nitric oxide production (https://www.mskcc.org/cancer-care/integrative-medicine/herbs/olive-leaf). A separate study on cardiovascular health in overweight individuals also found olive leaf phenolics positively affected CVD risk factors including high blood pressure (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8137474/).

**Bottom line:** Evidence suggests olive leaf extract *can* modestly reduce blood pressure, but higher-quality, larger trials are needed before it can be recommended as a reliable treatment.
